title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: sex My outcome: income >= 50000
Question A: “Of each sex (group), what share has at least $50,000? (outcome)?” Question B: “Of everyone with an income of at least $50,000 (outcome), what share is each sex? (group)?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = sex,
    has_outcome = income >= 50000
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  group  has_outcome     n
  <chr>  <lgl>       <int>
1 Female FALSE        1776
2 Female TRUE          654
3 Male   FALSE        1473
4 Male   TRUE         1097




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)







Figure 1: Share of each group with the outcome.





I predicted that males would have a higher rate of income above $50,000 than females. The plot allows me to compare the percentage of each group that reaches this income level. Each bar represents its own group’s total, making it possible to compare groups fairly even when they have different numbers of people.


A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)







Figure 2: Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size.





The standard error ranges show how much uncertainty there is around each group’s estimated rate. A smaller group will generally have a wider range because it has fewer observations. This helps readers recognize that smaller groups are still important and should not be ignored when comparing outcomes.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group      n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Male    2570
2 Female  2430

a3_start <- min(a3_table$n) / 2

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 1.054475

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 3: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 1.1.
The original plot shows the full difference in group sizes starting from zero. The zoomed plot makes the difference easier to see but can make it appear larger than it really is. The filtered plot removes part of the scale and can be misleading because it hides some of the original data. I would publish the original plot because it shows the group sizes without exaggerating the difference.


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)







Figure 4: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





Question A compares the percentage within each sex, while question B compares how much each sex contributes to everyone who meets the income outcome. The results can point in the same direction, but they measure different things because the groups may have different sizes. Question A is the better choice when comparing income rates between groups.

Figure 5: Share of each group with the outcome.





The plot shows the percentage of pitches that resulted in strikes for each pitch type. Shares are more useful than raw counts because some pitch types may have been thrown much more often than others.

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Average pitch speed", y = NULL)
